chromatic.constantStructure@1.1.summary: Plane into D7(♯5) with its own shape from above: B♭maj7 → E7(♯5) → E♭7(♯5) → D7(♯5).
chromatic.constantStructure@1.1.deepDive: Constant structure keeps one chord shape and moves it in parallel, so the ear follows the shape rather than a key. B♭maj7 keeps the downbeat, then D7(♯5)'s exact shape slides down by half steps (E → E♭ → D). Every voice moves a semitone at a time, the smoothest voice leading there is, while the passing chords come from outside the key.
chromatic.constantStructure@1.1.recreateRule: Near the end of a chord, play the next chord's exact shape a half step (or a whole step) above it and slide the whole hand down into it.

functional.secondaryTwoFive@2.1.summary: Replace D7(♯5) with the target's own ii–V: Fm9 → B♭7(♭9) → E♭maj7.
functional.secondaryTwoFive@2.1.deepDive: E♭maj7 is the IV chord. Putting its own ii–V in front briefly makes it sound like home: B♭ is a perfect 5th above E♭, and F is a 5th above that. The guide tones barely move: A♭ → A♭ → G, E♭ → D → D. You give up the colour of D7(♯5) and get the strongest pull in tonal harmony instead: the root falls a 5th, twice.
functional.secondaryTwoFive@2.1.recreateRule: Any major or minor chord can get its own ii–V: from the target, go up a 5th for the V and another 5th for the ii.

voicing.upperStructureBVI@2.1.summary: Same chord, new voicing: a B♭ major triad over a D–C–F♯ shell gives D7(♯9,♭13).
voicing.upperStructureBVI@2.1.deepDive: The left hand holds only what defines the dominant: the root, the ♭7 (C) and the 3rd (F♯). The right hand plays a plain B♭ triad (B♭ D F), which over D reads as ♭13, root and ♯9. The shape is easy and the tension is high. B♭ and D are already in E♭maj7, so the resolution is effortless.
voicing.upperStructureBVI@2.1.recreateRule: Over a dominant, play the major triad built on its ♭13 (a major 3rd below the root) above a root–♭7–3 shell. You get a 7(♯9,♭13).

chromatic.commonToneDiminished@3.1.summary: Lean into E♭maj7 from the diminished chord on the same root: E♭dim7 → E♭maj7.
chromatic.commonToneDiminished@3.1.deepDive: E♭dim7 shares only its root with E♭maj7. Its G♭ and B♭♭ (heard as ♯2 and ♯4) each rise a half step, into G and B♭, the 3rd and 5th. It's an appoggiatura chord: tension that dissolves into the chord you were already on, so it adds motion without changing the harmony.
chromatic.commonToneDiminished@3.1.recreateRule: On a major chord that lasts a while, start with the diminished 7th on the same root and let it resolve up by half steps.

dominant.tritoneSub@4.1.summary: Swap G7(♯5) for D♭9, the dominant a tritone away.
dominant.tritoneSub@4.1.deepDive:
G7(♯5) and D♭9 share the same tritone: B–F (3rd and ♭7 of G7) are C♭–F (♭7 and 3rd of D♭7), the same keys spelled differently. That interval is what makes a dominant want to resolve, so the substitute still lands on Cm7. The difference is the bass, which now slides down a half step (D♭ → C) instead of falling a 5th.

D♭ Lydian dominant uses exactly the same 7 notes as G altered: both are modes of A♭ melodic minor. Soloing over the sub is the same as playing altered over the original.
dominant.tritoneSub@4.1.recreateRule: Any dominant 7 can be replaced by the dominant 7 a tritone (♭5) away. The 3rd and ♭7 swap roles, and the bass moves by a half step.

functional.secondaryTwoFive@6.1.summary: Put the related ii in front of the dominant: Dm7♭5 → G7(♭9) → Cm7.
functional.secondaryTwoFive@6.1.deepDive: G7(♯5) already resolves down a 5th to Cm7. Every dominant has a "related ii", the minor chord a 5th above its root. Inserting it turns one chord into a full ii–V and doubles the forward motion. The target is minor, so the ii is half-diminished (Dm7♭5), borrowed from C harmonic minor. Guide tones: F → F → E♭, C → B → B♭.
functional.secondaryTwoFive@6.1.recreateRule: Any dominant can borrow its related ii: the minor 7 chord a 5th above its root (m7♭5 if the target is minor).

symmetric.coltraneSubstitution@7.1.summary: Turn Cm7 → F7 → B♭maj7 into a tour of three keys a major 3rd apart: Cm7 → D♭7 → G♭maj7 → A7 → Dmaj7 → F7 → B♭maj7.
symmetric.coltraneSubstitution@7.1.deepDive: Coltrane's substitution divides the octave into three equal parts. G♭, D, B♭ are a major 3rd apart (an augmented triad), and each is reached from its own dominant (D♭7, A7, F7). You pass through three key centres in the time of one ii–V and still land on B♭maj7. Practise the guide tones first: E♭ → D♭ → D♭ → C♯ → C♯ → C → B♭, B♭ → C♭ → B♭ → A → A → A → A.
symmetric.coltraneSubstitution@7.1.recreateRule: Over ii–V–I, tonicize the keys a major 3rd apart: V7–I into ♭VI, V7–I into III, then the real V7–I.

gospel.halfStepTurnaround@8.1.summary: F7 → B♭maj7 becomes E♭/F → B13(♯11) → B♭maj9.
gospel.halfStepTurnaround@8.1.deepDive: E♭/F is a F9sus: a E♭ triad over F. It's the gospel way to sound the dominant while holding back the 3rd. B13(♯11) is the tritone sub of F7, voiced as a 13(♯11) cluster a half step above B♭. Each voice either slides down a half step or stays put as it lands on B♭maj9.
gospel.halfStepTurnaround@8.1.recreateRule: Before a tonic, play a 13(♯11) chord a half step above it and slide the whole shape down. Put IV/V in front (a triad on the dominant's ♭7, over its root) for the sus colour.

modal.backdoorTwoFive@8.1.summary: Come in through the back door: E♭m7 → A♭9 → B♭maj7, instead of F7 → B♭maj7.
modal.backdoorTwoFive@8.1.deepDive: E♭m7 and A♭9 are borrowed from B♭ minor (iv and ♭VII7). A♭9 has no leading tone. Its ♭7 (G♭) falls a half step to F, the 5th of B♭, its 3rd (C) moves a step into the tonic chord, and the root rises a whole step home. It's a darker, bluesier cadence than F7 → B♭maj7, with no tritone resolving.
modal.backdoorTwoFive@8.1.recreateRule: For a major I, approach from iv m7 → ♭VII7: the minor chord a 4th above the tonic, then the dominant a whole step below it.

modal.flatSixFlatSeven@8.1.summary: Replace the dominant with two borrowed chords whose roots climb into the tonic: G♭maj7 → A♭6 → B♭maj7.
modal.flatSixFlatSeven@8.1.deepDive: G♭maj7 and A♭6 come from B♭ Aeolian, the parallel minor. The roots rise by whole steps (G♭ → A♭ → B♭), so the arrival feels inevitable without a dominant chord or a tritone anywhere. It's a bright, open cadence that suits the end of a phrase and tags at the end of a tune.
modal.flatSixFlatSeven@8.1.recreateRule: Before a major tonic, play the major chords on ♭6 and ♭7 of the key and let the bass climb by whole steps into I.
